title: The leap
hookLine: the ocean to Lanka; the mountain that offers rest; no rest till Rama's work is done
carry: no rest till rama's work is done

lines: A MOUNTAIN RISES: REST ON ME.
cards: Hanuman climbs a mountain on the shore and grows huge. He presses down so hard that the rocks crack and the trees shake loose their flowers. Then he jumps.
The text makes a spectacle of it: blossoms pulled along behind him, his shadow racing over the waves like a ship. He's flying to Lanka to find Sita.
Halfway across, a mountain named Mainaka rises out of the sea, and speaks. You're doing a great thing for a good cause. Rest on me.
Eat some fruit. A kind offer, from a real mountain, right there.

teach.b: Hanuman thanks the mountain. He touches it politely with his hand and says: I've made a promise; I can't stop. And he flies on.
Centuries later the poet Tulsidas gave him a line here that Hindi speakers still quote: without finishing Rama's work, where is rest for me? The next test comes straight after.
The gods send Surasa, mother of serpents, to see what he's made of. She rises from the water, mouth open: nobody passes me without going in. Hanuman grows bigger.
Then he shrinks to the size of a thumb, darts into her mouth and straight back out, and bows. I went in. Now let me go.
Surasa laughs and blesses him. A third test follows, Simhika, a creature who grabs shadows, and he gets past her too. Now remember what he said before he jumped.

teach.h: LIKE AN ARROW SHOT BY RAMA.
teach.b: Valmiki has him say he'll fly to Lanka like an arrow shot by Rama. That's the secret of the leap. It isn't Hanuman's errand.
It's Rama's work, and Rama's work carries him. This whole journey is the Sundara Kanda, the beautiful book, the fifth book of the Ramayana, Hanuman's book.
Many Hindu families read it whole in hard times or before a big step, because it's the book where a devotee crosses what no one can cross, doing God's work.

teach.h: NO REST TILL RAMA'S WORK IS DONE.
teach.b: No rest till Rama's work is done.

how: Some Hindus read or recite the Sundara Kanda, the Ramayana's book of Hanuman's journey, as a devotional practice, sometimes in full over a day or across several days, especially in difficult times.

o: one giant jump that carries Hanuman straight to the princess
Hanuman's flight over the ocean, with tests along the way
a test of strength Hanuman passes to serve the prince

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Hanuman beats Surasa by growing bigger than her
she keeps opening wider. he wins by shrinking to a thumb and darting in and out.
he touches the mountain politely, thanks it, and flies on: Rama's work first.
some Hindus recite the Sundara Kanda in hard times
the fifth book, Hanuman's, is read whole as a devotion.

games.q: you're Hanuman. Surasa blocks the sky: nobody passes without entering her mouth. every time you grow, she opens wider. what do you do?
o: keep growing until she gives up.
shrink to the size of a thumb, dart in and out, and bow.
turn back and find another route.
games.why: he gets small and quick. Surasa laughs and blesses him. not everything is won by getting bigger.

practice: Sit and breathe. Name one thing you keep meaning to start: a call, a class, a hard conversation.
If you pray, offer it before you begin, the way Hanuman flew as Rama's arrow: say Shri Ram, or the name of God you use, and give the first step to God. If you don't pray, name who it's really for.
Then picture just the first moment of the leap.

wordCard.voice: The leap. The ocean to Lanka, flown as Rama's arrow: a mountain thanked and passed, and Surasa outwitted by getting small.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the beautiful book, the fifth book of the Ramayana, about Hanuman's journey.

carryVoice: Your line: no rest till Rama's work is done. Hanuman flew as Rama's arrow. That's thirty-two days.
